title: Why build a bad pipeline first

beats.say: Why would anyone build a deliberately bad pipeline first?

Picture plumbing a new house. You could buy beautiful taps first. But you only find leaks when water runs through every pipe and joint. So a plumber first connects one plain pipe from the street to the sink, and turns the water on.

A walking skeleton is that plain pipe for data. Trip events go in one end, get counted, and land in a table you can ask questions of. Every piece is the simplest thing that works. Meridian, a ride company, wants completed trips per city, per hour, by Friday.
The leaks are rarely inside one tool. They hide at the joints, where one tool hands data to the next. A thin pipeline running end to end shows you those joints early.

show.title: Where problems live
items: Thin and end to end shows them early

check.q: Why build every stage as the simplest thing that works before improving any of them?
opts: Simple tools are always cheaper
It exposes problems at the joints between tools early
It removes the need for testing later
check.why: Problems mostly appear where tools hand data to each other. A thin end to end version shows those early, before you polish any one part.

work: Before polishing any one component, get a dummy record flowing from source to final query.
List each hand-off in your current pipeline and ask what could break at each.

title: The skeleton pipeline, step by step

beats.say: What is the smallest pipeline that can answer: how many trips completed, per city, per hour?

show.text: Completed trips per city, per hour

beats.say: First, a script makes fake trip events, around one hundred a second, and writes them to a Kafka topic called trip events. Kafka is a log. It keeps events in order, so other tools can read them whenever they are ready.

Every hour, Airflow, a scheduler, starts a Spark job. Spark reads that hour, keeps only completed trips, groups by city, and writes Parquet files to object storage. Parquet stores data by column, so queries read only what they need.

Then plain SQL counts completed trips per city. Airflow also checks the row count. One hour is about three hundred sixty thousand events, so zero rows means something broke, and the run should fail loudly.

check.q: What is the job of the row count check in the Airflow DAG?
opts: It speeds up the Spark job
It makes a silent empty result fail loudly
It deletes duplicate events from Kafka
check.why: A job can succeed technically yet write nothing. A row count check turns that silent failure into a visible one.

work: Add a minimum row count assertion to the end of one scheduled job.
Draw your own pipeline as boxes and label what format sits between each pair.

title: Where the skeleton breaks

beats.say: Your hourly job died halfway and Airflow retried it. Did Meridian just count trips twice?

show.sub: the joints are where it breaks

beats.say: Possibly. If the retry appends new files beside the half-written ones, those trips are counted twice. The fix is idempotency. Rerunning the same hour overwrites that hour's partition, so the answer is the same however many times it runs.

Next, small files. A job that writes every few minutes leaves thousands of tiny Parquet files. Each one costs a metadata lookup, so queries slow down. Compact them into files of a few hundred megabytes.
Last, late data. A trip completed at 10:59 may arrive at 11:05. An hourly job that cut off at 11:00 misses it. Decide whether you group by event time or arrival time, and how long you wait.

show.title: Late data decisions
items: Event time: when the trip happened
Arrival time: when we saw it
Wait window before closing the hour

check.q: An hourly Spark job fails halfway and is retried. What makes the retry safe?
opts: Appending output files on every run
Overwriting that hour's partition so reruns give the same result
Running the job twice and averaging the counts
check.why: Idempotent writes mean a rerun replaces the same output, so retries cannot create duplicates.

work: Check whether your retried jobs overwrite a partition or append, and fix any that append.
Measure file count and average file size on your largest table.
Write down your lateness rule: event time or arrival time, and the wait window.

title: Is the skeleton the right design?

beats.say: Meridian only needs hourly counts. So why run Kafka, Spark and Airflow at all?

show.text: Do you need all of this?

beats.say: Honestly, at one hundred events a second, one Postgres table and a cron job would answer this. Kafka and a Spark cluster cost money around the clock, and someone must be on call for them.
The skeleton is not the final design. It is a test rig. You swap one part at a time, such as batch for streaming, and rerun the same end to end check to see what that one swap changed.

show.title: Swap one part at a time

beats.say: Keep Kafka when several teams need replay or the rate hits tens of thousands a second. Otherwise, choose the boring option, and say why in the interview.

show.title: Choose by need
items: Replay or many consumers: keep Kafka
Tens of thousands of events a second: keep Kafka
Otherwise: the boring option, and justify it

check.q: What is the best use of the walking skeleton once it works?
opts: Ship it unchanged as the final design
Use it as a test rig and swap one component at a time
Rebuild everything at once for production
check.why: Changing one part at a time against the same end to end check shows exactly what each choice costs or gains.

work: For your current stack, write the simplest alternative and the volume at which it would stop working.
Keep one end to end test that you rerun after every component change.

title: The conveyor belt of the terminal

beats.say: How can one line of typing sort a forty gigabyte log on a laptop with only sixteen gigabytes of memory?
Think of a factory conveyor belt. Items pass one at a time. Each worker does one small job, then hands the item along. Nobody ever holds the whole pile.

show.title: A *belt* moves one item at a time

beats.say: The terminal pipe works the same way. One tool reads a line. The next counts it. The next sorts the counts. The file flows through like items on a belt, so memory stays small.
And Git is your saved history, like versions of a document, so you can try changes safely.

check.q: Why can a pipe handle a file bigger than memory?
opts: It compresses the file first
It processes the file a line at a time and passes results along
It copies the file to the cloud
check.why: Each tool reads a small piece, does its job and hands it on, so the whole file is never held in memory.

work: Run head dash n 3 on a data file before loading it anywhere.
Try a two-step pipe on a small file to feel the streaming idea.

title: Counting values with a pipe

beats.say: You have a three million row trips file. How do you find the most common value in column three without opening it?
Cut pulls out column three, one line at a time. Sort groups equal values side by side. Uniq dash c collapses each group into a count.
Then sort dash r n orders the counts from biggest to smallest, and head keeps the top ten. Only ten lines reach your screen.

show.title: Value counts
show.text: cut -d, -f3 trips.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

beats.say: Before that, use head dash n three with jq to peek at records, and wc dash l to count rows. Peek first, so you never load a huge file blindly.

check.q: In the value count pipe, what does the first sort do?
opts: Puts the biggest counts first
Places equal values next to each other so uniq can count them
Removes duplicate rows
check.why: Uniq only merges neighbouring identical lines, so sort must bring equal values together first.

work: Run a value count on a low-cardinality column of a real file.
Use du dash sh with sort dash h to find what is eating disk.

title: Git commands for the right situation

beats.say: You pushed a bad commit to main. Do you rewrite history, or add to it?
On shared branches, add to it. Git revert creates a new commit that undoes the old one. Everyone's copies still match, so nothing breaks for teammates.
Rewriting is for local work only. Git reset soft head tilde one removes your last local commit but keeps the changes staged. Do it before you push, never after.

Start each change on its own branch with git switch dash c. Park half-done work with git stash. When something broke and you don't know when, git bisect binary searches history. A thousand commits needs about ten checks.

check.q: A bad commit is already pushed to shared main. What is the safest fix?
opts: git reset --soft HEAD~1 and force push
git revert with the commit id
Delete the repository and re-clone
check.why: Revert adds a new commit that undoes the change, so teammates' history is never rewritten.

work: Practice revert, stash and bisect on a throwaway repository.
Name branches by change, such as feature slash ingest.

title: Why a tidy one-liner can lie

beats.say: Why can your tidy one-liner give a wrong answer on a perfectly healthy CSV?
Cut splits on every comma. If a quoted field contains a comma, like Smith, John, the columns shift and your counts are quietly wrong. Use a real CSV tool for those files.
Also, wc dash l counts newlines, not records. A record spanning lines, or a missing final newline, changes the number. And grep dash c counts matching lines, not distinct events.

Streaming has limits too. Sort must see everything before it outputs, so it spills temporary files to disk. Fill that disk and the job fails. Uniq only merges neighbours, so skipping sort gives wrong counts.

check.q: Why might a pipe over a 40 GB file still fail even though it streams?
opts: Pipes cannot read large files
Sort must see all data and can fill the temporary disk
Head loads the whole file
check.why: Sort cannot output until it has read everything, so it spills to temp files; a full disk stops the job.

work: Check free space in the temp directory before sorting very large files.
Use a CSV-aware tool when fields may contain quoted commas.

title: When to leave the shell behind

beats.say: When does a shell one-liner stop being the right tool?

When you need repeatable, tested, scheduled logic. A one-liner has no schema, no retries and no review trail. Once a check matters to the business, move it into a pipeline job, or a SQL query in an engine like DuckDB or Spark.

Remote storage adds cost. Listing an S3 prefix recursively makes paged list calls, slow and billed across millions of objects. Pulling data down just to count it adds transfer charges. Prefer inventory reports, or query the data where it lives.

show.title: Cost on object storage
items: Recursive ls is many list calls
Use S3 inventory or query in place

beats.say: For history, rebase keeps main linear but rewrites commits, so use it only on your own branch. Choose merge when others share the branch.

check.q: Which is the best way to count objects in a huge S3 prefix regularly?
opts: Recursive ls from a laptop each time
Download everything and run wc
Use an inventory report or query the data in place
check.why: Inventory or in-place queries avoid millions of list calls and transfer costs, and they can be scheduled.

work: Promote any shell check that people rely on into a tested, scheduled job.
Set a team rule: rebase only unpushed personal branches.

title: A library and a coat check

beats.say: What if your files were stored like books in a library, with one librarian who knows where every page is?
That librarian is the NameNode in HDFS. A big file is cut into chunks, and each chunk is copied onto three different shelves. If one shelf collapses, the librarian notices and makes a new copy.

Object storage, like S3, is different. It is one giant coat check. You hand over a bag, get a tag, and later show the tag to get the bag back. There are no folders, only long tag names with slashes in them.

check.q: In the coat check picture of object storage, what is a folder?
opts: A real shelf holding many bags
Just part of a long tag name
A second librarian
A copy of the bag
check.why: Object storage is a flat map from key to object. Slashes in a key are only characters, so a folder is only a naming habit.

work: Explain HDFS and S3 to a colleague using the library and coat check pictures.
Look at one S3 path in your project and point out which parts are really just the key.

title: How HDFS keeps a file alive

beats.say: How does a one gigabyte file survive a machine dying?

show.sub: one machine dies. Is it gone?

beats.say: HDFS cuts it into eight blocks of 128 megabytes. Each block is copied to three different machines, so the cluster holds twenty four block copies.

show.title: Block copies for a 1 GB file

beats.say: The NameNode keeps the map of which DataNode holds which block, in memory. To read, you ask the NameNode for locations, then pull bytes straight from the DataNodes.

chip.text: Metadata and data take separate paths

beats.say: DataNodes send a heartbeat every three seconds. If one goes silent, the NameNode orders new copies of its blocks, so every block is back to three copies.

check.q: A client wants to read a file in HDFS. Where do the file bytes come from?
opts: Through the NameNode
Directly from DataNodes after asking the NameNode for locations
From the standby NameNode
From a temporary directory
check.why: The NameNode only answers where blocks are. Keeping bytes off it stops it becoming a bottleneck.

work: Work out how many blocks and copies a 10 GB file creates on your cluster.
Check the replication factor and block size configured for your main data directory.

title: Flat keys and the slow rename

beats.say: Why can renaming a folder take a blink on one system and an hour on another?
Object storage is a flat map from a key to an object. A key like raw, trip events, date, part one dot parquet is one long string. The slashes are just characters.
So renaming a folder means copying every object to a new key, then deleting the old one. Ten thousand files means twenty thousand calls, and the whole thing is not atomic.
In HDFS the same rename is one metadata change inside the NameNode. It is instant, and it happens all or nothing.

check.q: Why is renaming a prefix on S3 slow?
opts: The NameNode is overloaded
Each object must be copied and the old one deleted
S3 locks the whole bucket
Rename compresses the data
check.why: There are no real directories. A rename is a copy and a delete per object, so cost grows with file count.

work: Find any job in your pipelines that renames output directories on S3.
Count how many objects sit under one output prefix to estimate the cost of a rename.

title: A million tiny files

beats.say: Why can a million tiny files hurt a cluster that stores petabytes?

show.sub: the disks are empty, yet the cluster is sick

beats.say: Every file and every block is an object in NameNode memory, roughly 150 bytes each. Ten million small files means about twenty million objects, around three gigabytes of heap, before any real data moves.
The disks sit nearly empty, but the NameNode runs out of memory. Each small file also becomes its own task, so jobs spend more time starting than working.

chip.text: Memory, not disk, is the limit

beats.say: The fix is compaction: merge small files into files of hundreds of megabytes. And remember the NameNode is the one part you cannot lose, so run a standby.

show.title: Defences
items: Aim for hundreds of MB per file

check.q: What is the main resource that millions of small files exhaust in HDFS?
opts: Disk space on DataNodes
NameNode memory
Network bandwidth between racks
Replication factor
check.why: Each file and block is a NameNode memory object, so file count matters more than total bytes.

work: Report file count and average file size for your busiest directories.
Schedule a compaction job for any directory with files under 64 MB.

title: Half a result on object storage

beats.say: A job finished, yet a reader saw only half of its output. How?

show.sub: a reader saw some files, not all

beats.say: Old Hadoop jobs wrote to a temporary directory, then renamed it into place. On HDFS that is one atomic step, so output appears all at once.
On S3 that rename is a copy and delete per object. A reader listing the folder midway sees some files new and some missing. A crash leaves a half result behind.
Table formats like Iceberg and Delta commit by swapping one small metadata pointer. Readers see the old version or the new one, never a mix.

show.title: Pointer swap commit
items: Readers see old or new, never both

check.q: Why do Iceberg and Delta avoid the half result problem?
opts: They rename faster
They commit by atomically swapping a small metadata pointer
They replicate files three times
They lock the bucket
check.why: Data files are invisible until the pointer changes, so a single small atomic update publishes everything.

work: Check whether any job publishes by renaming a prefix on S3, and flag it as a risk.
Read how your table format commits, and write down what a reader sees mid-write.

title: Choosing HDFS or object storage

beats.say: When would you still pick HDFS over S3 for a new design?

show.sub: default to one, justify the other

beats.say: Default to object storage. Compute and storage scale separately, so you can switch compute off at night and pay only for bytes. HDFS bills for the whole cluster, and three copies mean one terabyte of data uses three terabytes of disk.

show.title: Disk needed for 1 TB of data

beats.say: HDFS still wins on premises, where you already own the machines, or when you need data next to compute and cheap, fast renames and appends.
Object storage also charges per request, so millions of tiny files become a slow bill. Use large Parquet files plus a table format.

check.q: Which reason best justifies choosing object storage for a new analytics platform?
opts: Atomic directory renames
Compute and storage scale and are paid for independently
No need to think about file sizes
Data always sits next to the compute
check.why: Separating compute from storage lets you scale or switch off compute while paying only for stored bytes. Renames are weaker, and file size still matters.

work: Estimate the monthly cost of your cluster against bytes stored plus requests on S3.
Write a one page note listing where your platform depends on atomic rename, and what replaces it.

title: The receipt roll that never tears

beats.say: What if a messaging system never threw a message away after you read it?

show.sub: Kafka does not delete on read

beats.say: Picture a shop's receipt roll. Every sale is printed at the bottom, one after another, and nothing is ripped off. That is Kafka: a log, which just means a list you only ever add to.
Each receipt has a number, called its offset. Each reader keeps a bookmark at the last number they read. Accounting reads at its own pace. Marketing reads the same roll too.
If a report turns out wrong, move the bookmark back and read again. The roll is still there. That is replay, and it is why data engineers love it.

show.title: Why it matters
items: Many readers, each with a bookmark

check.q: In the receipt roll analogy, what does moving a bookmark back let you do?
opts: Delete old receipts
Read the same messages again
Make the roll shorter
check.why: Reading does not remove messages, so resetting your position replays them. That is Kafka's replay.

work: Explain Kafka to a colleague using the receipt roll in one minute.
List two teams in your company who could read the same stream independently.

title: Topics, partitions and keys

beats.say: Meridian produces millions of trip events. How does Kafka keep one trip's events in order?

The stream is a topic, called trip events. A topic is split into partitions. Each partition is an ordered log on a broker, which is a Kafka server. Every message gets an offset, its position: zero, one, two.

The producer picks the partition. With a key, it hashes the key, meaning it turns it into a number. Then it divides by the partition count and keeps the remainder. Same trip id, same number, same partition.
So requested, accepted, started and completed for trip forty-two all land in one partition, in order. Order holds inside a partition, and nowhere else.

check.q: Why do all events for one trip_id arrive in order?
opts: Kafka sorts every topic globally
The key hashes to the same partition, and a partition is ordered
Consumers sort by timestamp
check.why: Same key gives the same partition, and Kafka guarantees order only inside a partition.

work: Check which key your busiest topic uses and what ordering it protects.
Write down the partition count of each topic you own.

title: Consumer groups and replay

beats.say: A topic has six partitions and you start ten consumers. How many actually work?
A consumer group shares the partitions among its members. Each partition goes to exactly one consumer in the group. So six partitions keep six consumers busy, and the other four sit idle.
The group records progress by committing offsets, which means saving the note: I have read up to here. If a consumer crashes, another one picks up from the last commit.
Reading does not delete. Messages stay for the retention period, say seven days. Fix a Spark bug, reset the offsets, and read the same data again.

show.title: Replay
items: Messages kept for retention, say 7 days
Fix the bug in the Spark job
Reset offsets, reprocess the same data

check.q: A topic has 4 partitions and a group has 6 consumers. What happens?
opts: All 6 share the work equally
4 work and 2 are idle
Kafka adds 2 partitions automatically
check.why: Each partition is read by one consumer in the group, so parallelism is capped at the partition count.

work: Compare consumer count to partition count for each of your groups.
Find out your topics' retention and whether it covers your longest outage.

title: Changing partitions and committing safely

beats.say: You double a topic from six to twelve partitions. Why might trip events now arrive out of order?

The key maps to a partition using the partition count. Change the count and the same trip id can hash somewhere new. New events go to a different partition than old ones, and two consumers may handle them at once.
Keyed randomly, it is worse. A consumer can see completed before started, because order only exists inside one partition.

show.title: Random keys
items: Events for one trip spread across partitions

beats.say: Another gotcha: commit offsets before you finish processing, and a crash loses messages. Commit after, and a crash means duplicates, so make your writes safe to repeat.

show.title: Commit timing
items: Commit before work: crash loses data
Commit after work: crash repeats data
Make writes idempotent, safe to repeat

check.q: Why is adding partitions to a keyed topic risky?
opts: Old messages are deleted
The key may map to a different partition, breaking per-key order
Consumers stop committing offsets
check.why: The partition is derived from the key and the partition count, so a new count moves keys.

work: Pick a partition count with headroom up front so you never have to change it.
Make your sink writes idempotent, then test by replaying one hour.

title: When Kafka is the wrong tool

beats.say: Kafka is great, so why not use it for everything?
Partition count is your parallelism ceiling and hard to change safely. Size it with headroom, but not into the hundreds per topic, because each partition costs broker memory and slows recovery.
A hot key is another limit. If one big customer is the key, one partition gets most of the traffic, and one consumer becomes the bottleneck no matter how many you add.
Retention costs disk. A hundred megabytes a second for seven days is about sixty terabytes, before replication.
For a nightly batch from one database, files or a table are simpler. Choose Kafka when many readers need ordered, replayable events.

show.title: Choose Kafka when
items: Otherwise files or tables are simpler

check.q: Which workload is the weakest fit for Kafka?
opts: Many teams reading the same ordered trip events
One nightly export from a single database to a warehouse
Replaying a day of events after a bug fix
check.why: A single nightly batch has no need for multiple readers, ordering or replay, so files or a table are simpler and cheaper.

work: Estimate retention disk as rate times seconds times replication for your busiest topic.
Check partition traffic for skew from hot keys.

title: Spark as a restaurant kitchen

beats.say: You tell Spark to filter a billion rows, and nothing happens. Is it broken?

show.sub: A filter on a billion rows, and silence

beats.say: No. Picture a restaurant kitchen. The driver is the head chef. She reads your order and writes the plan. The executors are the cooks. Each cook works on one tray of ingredients at a time. That tray is called a partition.

chip.text: A partition is one tray of data

beats.say: Saying filter or join is just writing on the order pad. Nothing is cooked yet. These notes are called transformations. Saying count, show, or write is like shouting serve it. That is an action, and now the cooks start.

Why wait? Because the chef sees the whole order first. She will not peel carrots nobody ordered, and she trims ingredients early. Spark skips unused columns and filters early too, so less work gets done.

show.title: Why laziness helps
items: The chef sees the whole order first
Filter early, so less work is done

check.q: You write a filter and a join on a big table, but never call count, show or write. What does Spark do?
opts: Runs both immediately and stores the result
Nothing yet, it only records the plan
Runs the filter but waits on the join
check.why: Filter and join are transformations, which are lazy. Work starts only when an action such as count, show or write is called.

work: Explain to a teammate the difference between a transformation and an action using the kitchen picture.
Next time a Spark cell returns instantly, check whether it contained any action at all.

title: Tracing the hourly job end to end

beats.say: When your job reads a Kafka topic and writes Parquet, what actually runs, and when?

Your code builds a plan: read, parse the JSON, filter to the time window, add date and hour columns. All transformations, so nothing has run. The write at the end is the action. Only then does the driver optimise the plan and cut it into tasks.

Say the topic has twelve partitions. Spark reads each one as a separate data partition, so twelve tasks. With four cores across the executors, four tasks run at once, so three waves. Each task parses its slice and writes Parquet files into the date and hour folders.
Because the whole plan is visible, the optimiser drops columns nobody uses, and the time filter runs right after parsing, so rows outside the window never reach the write.

show.title: What the optimiser does
items: Runs the time filter right after parsing
Rows outside the window never reach the write

check.q: A topic has 12 partitions and the cluster has 4 cores in total. Roughly how does the read stage run?
opts: 12 tasks in one wave
12 tasks in about 3 waves of 4
4 tasks in 12 waves
check.why: One task per input partition gives 12 tasks. Four cores run four at a time, so about three waves.

work: Open the Spark UI for a job and match each stage's task count to its input partitions.
Compare task count with total cores to see how many waves your job needs.

title: Silent wrong answers in the skeleton

beats.say: Your count says one million rows, and your write saves a different number. How?

show.text: Count is not what you wrote

beats.say: Every action re-runs the plan from the source. Count reads Kafka. Write reads it again. With ending offsets set to latest, new events may have arrived between the two runs. Fix it by pinning explicit end offsets, or cache the result.

Bad data is quieter. If a JSON line is malformed, from json returns null, not an error. A timestamp that fails to parse also becomes null, and the time filter then drops that row. No exception, no warning, just missing events.
Two more traps. Collect pulls every row into the driver's memory, so a big table crashes it. And partitioning by date and hour with many tasks writes many tiny files, which slows every later read.

show.title: Two more traps
items: Collect on a big table crashes the driver
Many tasks times many folders means tiny files
Tiny files slow every later read

check.q: A malformed JSON line reaches from json in your job. What most likely happens?
opts: The job fails with a parse exception
The row becomes null fields and may be silently dropped by a later filter
Spark retries the line until it parses
check.why: In default mode from json returns null instead of failing, and a null timestamp then fails the time filter, so the row disappears without any error.

work: Count rows that parse to null and compare to total rows before writing; alert if the gap is nonzero.
Pin explicit start and end offsets for each batch run.
Check output folders for file counts and sizes after each run.

title: Is Spark the right tool here?

beats.say: Is Spark the right tool for an hourly job that reads a few gigabytes?

show.sub: An hourly job, a few gigabytes

beats.say: Maybe not. Spark pays a fixed cost: starting a cluster, scheduling, shuffling over the network. For a few gigabytes, one machine running DuckDB or plain SQL can finish sooner and cost far less. Spark wins when data outgrows one machine, or work needs many cores.

show.title: Rough time for a small job

beats.say: If you keep Spark, fix the reading. Scanning from earliest each hour grows cost forever. Record the end offsets of each run, and start the next run there. Or use streaming with an available-now trigger, which keeps offsets in a checkpoint and stops when caught up.

chip.text: Cost tracks new data, not history

beats.say: If you need seconds of latency, hourly batch is the wrong shape; consider a continuous stream engine like Flink. Choose by data size, latency needed, and who runs the cluster.

show.title: Choose by three questions
items: Who runs and pays for the cluster?

check.q: Your hourly job rereads the whole topic from earliest and runtime grows each week. What is the best fix?
opts: Add more executors
Track end offsets per run, or use a checkpointed available-now stream
Switch the output format to CSV
check.why: Rereading history makes cost grow with all data ever written. Resuming from saved offsets makes cost follow only new data.

work: Estimate your hourly data volume and test whether a single machine tool finishes it faster.
Store end offsets alongside each output batch so reruns are repeatable.
Write down the latency target before choosing between batch and streaming.

title: Airflow as a kitchen manager

beats.say: How does a kitchen get the soup ready before the lunch rush, every single day, without anyone shouting orders?

show.text: Soup ready by noon. Every day.

beats.say: A recipe card lists the steps and their order. Chop, then boil, then serve. Airflow calls that card a DAG: a set of tasks, the order between them, and a schedule.
A manager watches the clock and says what should start now. That is the scheduler. Someone then assigns each job to a cook or a station. That is the executor.
And a logbook records every step. When the soup is late, you can see exactly which step failed.

chip.text: Late soup? Find the failed step

check.q: In the kitchen analogy, what does the scheduler do?
opts: Cooks the food
Decides which jobs should start now
Stores the leftover ingredients
check.why: The scheduler is the manager watching the clock and deciding what should run. Workers, chosen by the executor, do the actual work.

work: Draw one of your nightly jobs as boxes and arrows, showing which step must finish before the next.
Write down who or what decides when each job starts today, and where its history is recorded.

title: Why a run starts after its interval

beats.say: The nine to ten o'clock run starts just after ten, not at nine. Why would a scheduler wait?
Because each run covers a data interval. The hourly run for nine to ten can only begin once that hour is over, so all of its data exists.

chip.text: Hour is complete, data is complete

beats.say: The scheduler checks each DAG, finds tasks whose upstream tasks succeeded, and queues them. The executor picks where they run: a local process, Celery workers, or one Kubernetes pod per task.
Every attempt is recorded as queued, running, success or failed, so you can see exactly what happened and when.

check.q: Why does the 09:00 to 10:00 hourly run start just after 10:00?
opts: The scheduler is always an hour slow
The run needs the whole interval to be complete first
Executors only start work on the hour
check.why: A run covers a finished data interval. Waiting until 10:00 passes means all the data for that hour exists.

work: For each DAG, write down its data interval and when its run really starts.
Check which executor your team runs and why it was chosen.

title: Tasks, operators and XCom in code

beats.say: How do two tasks hand work to each other without sharing a disk?

show.text: Task A finishes. Task B needs its result.

beats.say: In the example, ingest runs the Spark job for one hour and returns a row count. Check receives that number and fails the run if it is zero.
That number travels through XCom, Airflow's small message store. A row count or a file path fits. A million rows does not, because XCom lives in the metadata database.
Big data stays in storage. Tasks pass only a pointer to it. Retries are set to two, with two minutes between attempts, so a network blip heals itself without paging anyone.

show.title: Habits
items: Pass a path or a count

check.q: What should you pass between tasks using XCom?
opts: A file path or a row count
The full table of results
A copy of the Spark cluster logs
check.why: XCom is stored in the metadata database, so it suits small values like a path or count. Large data belongs in storage.

work: Find any task that returns a large object and change it to write to storage and return the path.
Set sensible retries and a retry delay in default args.

title: The now() trap

beats.say: A task failed at ten past ten, retried at quarter to eleven, and wrote different data. Why?

show.text: Same task. Same run. Different data.

beats.say: The task asked the clock. Calling now gives a different answer on every attempt, so the retry processed a different hour.
The fix is to use the interval Airflow passes in: data interval start and data interval end. Same run, same hour, on every attempt. That makes a retry safe to repeat.
The same rule powers catch up and backfill. A backfill reruns chosen dates on purpose. With now, last Tuesday's backfill would quietly process today.

check.q: A backfill of last Tuesday processed today's data. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The executor was too small
The task read the current time instead of its data interval
XCom was too large
check.why: Tasks that call now ignore which interval the run is for. Using the interval boundaries makes reruns and backfills reproducible.

work: Search your DAG code for now, today and utcnow, and replace them with interval values.
Make writes overwrite the hour's partition so a retry cannot duplicate rows.

title: Catchup surprises

beats.say: You deploy a new hourly DAG with a start date one year ago. Why does the cluster suddenly melt?
Catchup is true. The scheduler creates a run for every missed hour since the start date. That is about eight thousand seven hundred sixty runs, all wanting workers at once.
That is why the example sets catchup false. Only new intervals run. Choose true only when history should be built, and cap how many runs go at once.

show.title: Safer defaults
items: Use true only to build history

beats.say: Remember too that a retry reruns the same task. Writes must be safe to repeat: overwrite that hour's partition, do not append.

check.q: What does catchup true do for a DAG whose start date is far in the past?
opts: Skips all old intervals
Creates a run for every missed interval
Runs only the latest interval twice
check.why: Catchup makes the scheduler create a run for each missed interval since the start date, which can be thousands.

work: Review every DAG for catchup and set false unless history is wanted.
Set a limit on concurrent active runs before any large backfill.

title: When Airflow is the wrong tool

beats.say: When is Airflow the wrong tool? Knowing that separates a good architect from a fan.

Pick the executor by isolation and cost. Local runs on one machine, fine for a laptop. Celery keeps a pool of workers always on, so tasks start fast, but you pay for idle time. Kubernetes gives each task its own pod and dependencies, but adds seconds of startup.

Airflow is not a streaming engine. It starts batch runs per interval, so second-level latency belongs to Kafka and Flink. It is also not a data processor. Spark does the heavy lifting. Airflow triggers, waits and records.
At thousands of tasks an hour, the metadata database and scheduler become the bottleneck. Keep tasks coarse.

show.title: Scale limits
items: Metadata database load grows with task count
Scheduler loop slows with many DAGs

check.q: Which workload is the weakest fit for Airflow?
opts: A nightly warehouse load
Second-by-second event processing
An hourly Spark job with a row count check
check.why: Airflow orchestrates batch runs per interval. Second-level streaming latency belongs to engines like Kafka and Flink.

work: Write a one-page note on why your team picked its executor and what the idle or startup cost is.
Move any heavy data processing out of Airflow tasks into Spark or the warehouse.
Track task counts per hour and metadata database load as an early warning.

title: The detective and the runner

beats.say: Can an AI actually do things, or does it only talk?

show.sub: How an AI gets things done

beats.say: Picture a brilliant detective locked in a room. She cannot leave. She writes notes: bring me the case file. You are the runner. You fetch it and slide it under the door.
She reads it and asks for another. That back and forth is the agent loop. The model only asks. Your code does every action.
She stops when she can answer, or when you call time. Without a limit, she could send you out forever, and you pay for every trip.

check.q: In an agent loop, who actually runs the tool?
opts: The model, inside the AI service
Your own code, after the model asks
The user, by hand every time
check.why: The model only replies with a request naming a tool and arguments. Your code runs it and sends back the result.

work: Explain the loop to a teammate using the detective and runner picture.
List which actions in your pipelines you would let a model request, and which stay human only.

title: Five steps of the agent loop

beats.say: What really happens when an AI model uses a tool? Five steps, in a loop.

You send the conversation plus a list of tools. Each tool has a name, a description, and a schema that describes its inputs. The model replies with text, or a request to call one tool with chosen arguments.
Your code runs that function, adds the result to the conversation, and calls the model again. Each turn, the model sees everything so far.
For a failed Airflow task, that is often three turns. List the failed logs. Read the last eighty lines of one. Then answer. The loop ends when the reply is not a tool request, or after six turns.

check.q: When does the loop stop normally?
opts: When the tool returns any result
When the reply is not a tool request
After exactly one model call
check.why: A reply that is plain text instead of a tool request means the model has its answer. Your max turns limit is the backstop.

work: Trace one real agent run and count turns and tool calls.
Write each tool description so a stranger could tell when to use it.

title: Never trust the path

beats.say: Who chooses the file path your code reads? The model does. So what if it asks for a password file?

Treat anything the model supplies as untrusted input, like a web form. The code first resolves the path to its real absolute form, then checks the log folder is a parent. Resolving first matters, because dot dot segments would slip past a simple text check.
A blocked path raises an error. That error is not a crash. It goes back to the model as a tool result marked as an error, with the message. The model reads it and tries a valid path instead.

check.q: A tool raises an error because the model chose a bad path. What should the loop do?
opts: Crash the whole job
Return the message as an error tool result
Silently skip and answer anyway
check.why: Sending the error back lets the model see what went wrong and choose another path, while the failure stays contained.

work: Audit every tool argument and decide what could be abused if the model were tricked.
Add a test that feeds a path with dot dot segments and confirm it is rejected.

title: Limits and honest answers

beats.say: What happens if the model never decides it is finished?

It keeps calling tools. Every turn resends the whole conversation, so each call costs more than the last. A limit of six turns caps the spend. When it is hit, return a clear stopped message, never a guess.
Second trap: models want to please. If the prompt demands a cause and the logs show none, the model invents a believable one. So the prompt says: if the logs do not show the cause, say so.

show.title: Allow "I don't know"
items: Prompt gives explicit permission to say unknown

beats.say: Asking for the exact log line helps too. A claim you can check against evidence is hard to fake.

check.q: Why tell the model it may say the logs do not show the cause?
opts: It saves tokens on every call
A model forced to give a cause may invent one
It lets the model skip calling tools
check.why: Without permission to be uncertain, the model fills the gap with a plausible but unsupported cause.

work: Set a max turns value on every agent loop and log when it is reached.
Require evidence, such as a quoted line, in answers and spot check a few.

title: Agent or plain pipeline?

beats.say: Do you need an agent, or just one model call?

If the steps never change, find the failed log, read it, summarise, write plain code and call the model once. It is cheaper, faster and easier to test. Use a loop only when the next step depends on what the last one found.
A loop costs more. Each turn takes seconds and resends a growing history, so three turns cost well over one call. Keep tool output small, like eighty lines, not whole files.
Read-only tools limit damage to a wrong answer. A tool that changes things needs a human approval step in front of it, plus a budget and an audit log. Add capabilities one at a time.

show.title: Grow power slowly
items: Read-only: worst case is a wrong answer
Budget and audit log on every run

check.q: When is a full agent loop the better choice over a fixed pipeline?
opts: When every run follows the same steps
When the next step depends on what was found
When you want the lowest possible cost
check.why: Loops earn their extra cost and risk only when the path varies with the findings. Fixed paths are cheaper as plain code.

work: Review each LLM workflow you own and mark whether the steps are really fixed.
Define approval, budget and audit rules before adding any tool that changes state.

title: The elevator button and the tip jar

beats.say: Why does pressing an elevator button five times still bring just one elevator?
Because the button only says, I want to be here. Pressing again changes nothing. That property has a name: idempotent. Doing it twice leaves the same result as doing it once.
Now picture a tip jar. Every coin you drop makes the total bigger. If a data job works like a tip jar and gets run twice, every row is counted twice.

And data jobs do get run twice. They retry after failures, people rerun them after fixing bugs, and teams refill a whole month of history. So build jobs like the elevator button: same request, same result.

show.title: Why jobs run again
items: Manual rerun after a bug fix

check.q: Which job is idempotent?
opts: Adds 100 rows to a table each time it runs
Replaces the 09:00 data with the same 100 rows each time
Sends a counter that goes up by one per run
check.why: Replacing the same data leaves the same result after one run or ten. Adding or counting up changes the result on every run.

work: List which of your jobs get retried or rerun, and note how each one writes.
Ask of every job: if this ran twice, would the numbers change?

title: Three ways a rerun stays safe

beats.say: You rerun the nine o'clock hour, and suddenly every trip event appears twice. Why?
The naive write uses append mode. Append just adds new files. Say the hour holds one million rows. Run it twice and the partition holds two million.
Fix one: overwrite the partition you own. The nine o'clock run replaces the nine o'clock folder, and nothing else. Set partition overwrite mode to dynamic first.
Fix two: merge on a key. Match rows on event id. Update the ones that exist, insert the ones that do not. Rerun it ten times and you still get one million rows.

check.q: The 09:00 job runs three times with the same input. Which write gives one million rows each time?
opts: Append mode
Overwrite of the 09:00 partition
Appending, then counting rows later
check.why: Overwriting the partition replaces its content, so the count stays at one million. Append adds a copy on each run.

work: Find one job that uses append and decide whether overwrite or merge fits it.
Rerun a single hour twice in a test and compare row counts.

title: Where idempotent writes bite back

beats.say: One config line decides whether a rerun fixes one hour or wipes the whole table. Which one?

By default, overwrite is static. Writing the nine o'clock hour deletes every partition in the table first, then writes just that one. A month of history, gone. Setting partition overwrite mode to dynamic replaces only the partitions present in the new data.

The second trap is de-duplicating on read. Keeping one row per event id downstream makes the numbers look right, but the lake still holds duplicates, storage grows, and every reader must remember the rule. It is a second line of defence, not a fix.

show.title: Dedupe on read hides it
items: Every reader must remember the rule

beats.say: Third, merge needs a table format, because plain Parquet files cannot update a row in place.

check.q: You overwrite hour 09 with the default static mode on a table partitioned by date and hour. What happens?
opts: Only hour 09 is replaced
Every partition in the table is deleted, then hour 09 is written
The write fails because the partition exists
check.why: Static overwrite clears the whole table before writing. Dynamic mode limits the replacement to the partitions in the new data.

work: Check that dynamic partition overwrite is set in every job that uses overwrite.
Test an overwrite on a copy of the table before trusting it in production.

title: Choosing how to make reruns safe

beats.say: An interviewer asks how you make a pipeline safe to rerun. What is the two-part answer?

First, bind every run to a fixed interval. The run for nine o'clock always processes nine o'clock, from the scheduled time, never from the clock on the wall. Second, every write replaces or merges, never blindly appends.

Choose by shape. Event data that lands by time suits partition overwrite: it is cheap, with no key lookups. Merge fits when late or corrected rows touch old partitions, but it rewrites files and costs more at scale.
Keep de-duplication downstream as a safety net, and alert on duplicate counts. If you cannot name a key, do not pick merge; overwrite a coarser partition instead.

show.title: Guardrails
items: Dedupe downstream as a safety net
No stable key? Overwrite a coarser partition

check.q: Late corrections arrive for rows in partitions from last week. Which write fits best?
opts: Append the corrections
Merge on a key
Overwrite the whole table daily
check.why: Merge updates the exact rows that changed, even in old partitions. Append creates duplicates, and a full overwrite is costly and risky.

work: For each pipeline, write down its run interval and its write strategy in one line.
Add a duplicate-count check on the event key and alert when it is above zero.

title: Airflow is the head chef

beats.say: How does a company make sure fifty data jobs run in the right order, every night, without someone watching?
Think of a restaurant kitchen. The head chef does not cook. She calls out orders: start the sauce, then plate the fish, and if the oven breaks, tell someone. Airflow is that head chef for data jobs.
The cooks are the real engines, like Spark or the warehouse. Airflow only says what runs, when, and in what order. It retries a failed step, sends an alert, and keeps a record of every run.

show.title: What the chef does
items: Keeps a record of every run

beats.say: Compare that with cron, a plain alarm clock. It rings at a time, but it knows nothing about order, failures or history.

check.q: In the kitchen picture, what is Airflow's job?
opts: Doing the heavy cooking itself
Deciding what runs, when, and checking the result
Only ringing at a fixed time
check.why: Airflow orchestrates: the engines such as Spark or the warehouse do the work, while Airflow handles order, retries, alerts and history.

work: List your nightly jobs and write down which depend on which.
Find one job still run by cron and note what happens when it fails.

title: Intervals, start times and backfills

beats.say: An hourly job covers nine to ten o'clock. When does it actually start?

Just after ten. A run covers a data interval, and it fires once that interval is finished, because the data is only complete then. Its logical date is the interval start, nine o'clock. Old code treated that date as now, a classic bug.

show.title: A run fires at the *end* of its interval

beats.say: Now backfill last week. Airflow creates one run per hour, a hundred and sixty eight in all, each with its own interval, and feeds them through the concurrency limits.
This is safe only if each run reads and overwrites just its own hour. That is idempotency: rerun it and nothing doubles.

check.q: An hourly DAG's 09:00 to 10:00 run starts when?
opts: At 09:00, when the hour begins
Just after 10:00, when the interval is complete
Whenever the scheduler is free, regardless of time
check.why: A run covers a data interval and fires at its end, once the data is complete. The logical date is the interval start.

work: Search your DAGs for execution date used as the current time and replace it with the data interval.
Make every load overwrite its own partition, then test by rerunning one day twice.

title: Why heavy DAG files hurt everyone

beats.say: Why can one badly written DAG file slow down every pipeline in Airflow?
Because the DAG processor re-reads every DAG file about every thirty seconds, looking for changes. Any code at the top of the file runs on every read.
Say the top calls an API or queries a database. That call now happens thousands of times a day, and a slow one delays how fast the scheduler sees all DAGs, or hits the parse timeout.

show.title: A slow call *delays the scheduler's view*

beats.say: The fix: keep the top level to definitions only, and do real work inside tasks. Then watch the DAG processing duration metric.

show.title: The fix
items: API calls and queries go inside tasks

check.q: Where should a database query for a DAG's config run?
opts: At module level in the DAG file
Inside a task
In an import at the top of the file
check.why: Module-level code runs on every parse, about every 30 seconds, for every file. Work inside a task runs only when the task runs.

work: Grep your DAG folder for requests, database connects and big imports at module level.
Add an alert on DAG processing duration.

title: Sensors that hog workers

beats.say: A sensor waits six hours for a file. What does that cost?
In poke mode it holds a worker slot the whole time, doing nothing. Twenty waiting sensors can starve the real tasks. Reschedule mode frees the slot between checks.

A deferrable operator goes further. It hands the wait to the triggerer, a separate process that runs thousands of waits as lightweight async coroutines. A worker is picked up again only when the event arrives.
In Airflow three, assets remove many sensors altogether. A DAG simply runs when an upstream task updates the asset.

check.q: Why is a deferrable operator better than a poke-mode sensor for a long wait?
opts: It checks the file more often
It frees the worker slot and waits in the triggerer
It skips the file check entirely
check.why: The triggerer runs thousands of waits cheaply as async coroutines, and a worker is used only after the event arrives.

work: Count sensors in poke mode and move long waits to deferrable operators.
Where upstream is another DAG, try asset-based scheduling instead of a sensor.

title: Celery or Kubernetes executor

beats.say: Celery or Kubernetes: how do you pick an Airflow executor, the part that actually runs tasks?
Celery keeps warm worker processes pulling tasks from a queue. Tasks start fast, which suits many short jobs. But all tasks share the workers' image and resources, and you size the pool yourself.

chip.text: Fast start, you size the pool

beats.say: Kubernetes starts one pod per task. You get isolation, a custom image and resources for each task, and scaling to zero. The price is pod start time, seconds or more, on every task.
Many platforms run both: light, fast tasks on Celery, heavy or unusual ones in pods.

show.title: Hybrid setup
items: Heavy or odd tasks in pods

check.q: Which workload fits Celery best?
opts: A few tasks needing custom images and scale to zero
Thousands of short tasks that share one environment
A GPU job needing its own container
check.why: Celery's warm workers start tasks fast, ideal for many short, similar tasks. Heavy or special tasks fit pods better.

work: Measure your task duration and pod start time before choosing an executor.
Move one heavy or oddly-dependent task into its own pod and compare.

title: When to say no to Airflow

beats.say: When should an architect say no to Airflow?

Streaming or sub-minute work: use Kafka with Flink or Spark streaming. Moving the data inside tasks: let Spark, the warehouse or a copy tool do it, and keep tasks thin. A lone dbt project: the warehouse or dbt Cloud can schedule it.
Airflow is the control plane of batch, not the data plane. It tells engines what to run and checks the result. Its cost is the always-on scheduler, database and workers.
Move off when work turns event-driven, when Dagster or warehouse pipelines cover everything you schedule, or when a managed service is cheaper.

show.title: Time to move off
items: Dagster or warehouse pipelines cover it all

check.q: A team runs one dbt project and nothing else. What is the best call?
opts: Deploy a full Airflow cluster for it
Let the warehouse or dbt Cloud schedule it
Replace dbt with Spark tasks
check.why: A single dbt project does not need cross-system orchestration, so a built-in scheduler avoids running an always-on Airflow.

work: Audit your DAGs for tasks that move data themselves and push that work to Spark or the warehouse.
Estimate the monthly cost of your scheduler, database and workers against a managed option.

title: What Airflow 3 changes

beats.say: What changed in Airflow three that an upgrade plan must cover?

show.sub: what must your upgrade plan cover?

beats.say: Tasks no longer talk to the metadata database directly. They go through the Task SDK and an API server, which is safer and lets tasks run in other environments and languages.
DAGs are versioned, so a run keeps the code it started with, and the UI shows which version ran. Datasets became assets with event-driven scheduling.
SubDAGs and execution date are gone, so budget a code pass before upgrading.

check.q: What does DAG versioning in Airflow 3 give you?
opts: Faster parsing of all files
A run keeps the code version it started with
Automatic removal of old DAGs
check.why: Each run stays tied to the DAG code it started with, and the UI shows which version ran, which helps debugging.

work: Scan your code for SubDAGs and execution date before planning an upgrade.
Check whether any task connects straight to the metadata database.
